name: WhatsApp
seo_title: Is WhatsApp Safe for Kids? Parent's Guide (2026)
seo_description: Is WhatsApp safe for kids? The UK age limit, the risks in group chats, WhatsApp's new parental controls for teens, and the settings to change today.
lead: WhatsApp is how most children stay in touch with friends, family and school. It's been left out of the UK's planned under-16 social media ban, but that doesn't make it safe by default. Here's what I'd change.
answer: Mostly, with a couple of settings changed. Messages are private and encrypted, which protects your child but also means nobody moderates what's sent. The biggest risk is group chats: by default, anyone with your child's number can add them to one.

sections.heading: What is WhatsApp?
body: WhatsApp is Meta's messaging app for chats, voice and video calls, groups, Status updates and Channels. It now includes Meta AI, a chatbot.
The minimum age in the UK is 13 (it was lowered from 16 in 2024). For under-13s, parents can now set up a parent-managed account in some regions.

subsections.heading: Group adds
body: Anyone with your child's number can add them to a group without asking, because the setting starts on Everyone. That puts them in chats with people they don't know.

subsections.heading: Bullying in groups
body: Group chats are where a lot of bullying happens, out of sight. Children can be excluded, removed or targeted, and it follows them home.

subsections.heading: Harmful content
body: Any member can share explicit images, violent videos or harmful links, and everyone in the group receives them. End-to-end encryption means WhatsApp can't see or remove them.

subsections.heading: Disappearing messages
body: Disappearing and view-once messages can remove evidence before anyone sees it, and give a false sense that what's sent is gone. It can still be recorded on another device.

subsections.heading: Who can add them to groups
body: Settings, then Privacy, then Groups. Change Everyone to My contacts.

subsections.heading: Profile photo and Status
body: In Settings, then Privacy, set Profile photo, About and Status to My contacts.

subsections.heading: Disappearing messages
body: In each chat, tap the name at the top and check whether disappearing messages are on. Turn them off where you can.

subsections.heading: Read receipts
body: In Settings, then Privacy, turning off Read receipts can ease the pressure to reply straight away.

sections.heading: WhatsApp's parental controls

subsections.heading: For 13 to 17-year-olds
body: On your teen's phone, open Settings, then Parental controls, confirm their date of birth and link to your account. You set a PIN that's needed to loosen their privacy settings, you can limit Channels, Status and Meta AI, and you're told about things like new contacts. You can't read their messages.

subsections.heading: For under-13s
body: Parent-managed accounts, launched in March 2026, only allow messaging and calls. You approve who can contact them and which groups they join, behind a parent PIN.

after: Both are rolling out gradually, so they may not be on your phone yet. Your teen has to agree to link accounts.

sections.heading: Signs something's wrong
list: Being added to groups with people they don't know
Being left out of, or removed from, a group their friends are in
Checking their phone anxiously, or not wanting to go to school
Deleting chats, or being secretive about a group
Being asked for photos, or to keep a chat secret

sections.heading: What I'd do as a parent
body: Look through their group list together now and then: who's the admin, and do they know everyone in it? If something upsetting happens, the advice is the same every time: don't delete it, screenshot it, tell me, and report it. And explain that Meta AI isn't the place for personal or sensitive conversations.
list: "Which group chats are the most fun? Are there any you'd rather not be in?"
"Has anyone ever added you to a group you didn't want to be in?"
"If something nasty gets posted in a group, what would you do?"

teachers: If a pupil discloses harassment in a WhatsApp group, advise them not to delete messages and to screenshot before reporting, because WhatsApp itself keeps little. Low reporting doesn't mean low bullying: much of it happens in private group chats that staff never see.

faq.q: What age is WhatsApp for in the UK?
faq.a: 13. WhatsApp lowered its minimum age in the UK and Europe from 16 to 13 in 2024.

faq.q: How do I stop strangers adding my child to WhatsApp groups?
faq.a: In Settings, then Privacy, then Groups, change Everyone to My contacts.
Yes, since 2026: parental controls for 13 to 17-year-olds and parent-managed accounts for under-13s. They're rolling out gradually, and you can't read your child's messages with either.

faq.q: Is WhatsApp included in the UK under-16 social media ban?
faq.a: No. The government has said messaging apps such as WhatsApp won't be included.

help: Worried about a child right now? Childline is free and confidential on [0800 1111](tel:08001111), any time. You are not alone.
